title: The fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23)
hook: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control

segments.voice: Yesterday, charism: a gift of the Spirit, given for someone else's good. Your line was many gifts, one spirit. Whose quiet gift did you name out loud? Day one thousand ninety-four.

Nobody has ever heard an apple tree grunt. It doesn't clench its branches in spring and force the apples out. It stands in the sun, drinks the rain, stays rooted, and one day the fruit is just there. A gardener can water, prune and wait. A gardener can't make an apple. Yesterday Paul listed gifts: to one person this, to another that. Today he writes to different churches, the churches of Galatia, and the picture changes from a toolbox to an orchard. Today's words: the fruit of the Spirit.

Here's the verse in the King James: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law." Look at the first words closely. The fruit is. Not the fruits are. One fruit, with many flavors. Some readers hear it as one life growing all of these together, rather than a menu where you pick your favorite. Set that beside yesterday. Gifts are handed out differently: one person heals, another teaches. Some readers add that the fruit, unlike the gifts, is meant for everyone: nobody is let off love because their gift is administration. Now notice what Paul sets it against. Just before, he lists what he calls "the works of the flesh." Works on one side, fruit on the other. Works are made. Fruit grows. That's the heart of today's line. Then the old words. Longsuffering is patience that holds out a long time. Faith, here, is faithfulness, being someone others can count on. Meekness is gentleness, strength that doesn't push. Temperance is self-control. Read the list again in today's English and it sounds like a description of someone you'd want to live next door to. So is there no effort at all? Christians answer that in different ways. The same chapter also says, "Walk in the Spirit." Walking takes steps. Jesus, in John's Gospel, uses the picture of a vine: "I am the vine, ye are the branches," and the branch bears fruit by staying joined to the vine. Prayer, worship, scripture, sacraments, serving others: in Christian teaching these are like staying joined, like sun and rain. They don't manufacture fruit. They keep the branch connected. And that last phrase, "against such there is no law," has a smile in it. Try picturing a court that bans patience.
screen: `THE FRUIT IS, NOT THE FRUITS ARE.` · `GIFTS DIFFER; THE FRUIT IS FOR ALL.` · `WORKS ARE MADE. FRUIT GROWS.` · `STAY JOINED TO THE VINE.` · then, large: `AGAINST SUCH THERE IS NO LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one fruit for today. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Run slowly through the list: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Notice which one tugs at you, maybe because it's the one you're shortest on. Pick that one. Don't make a plan to squeeze it out of yourself. Instead, picture one moment later today where it could grow: a long line, a slow reply, a hard conversation. If you pray, you can ask for that fruit by name. If you don't, just keep the one word with you, like a seed in a pocket. The bell holds the time.
The fruit of the Spirit. One fruit with many flavors, grown, not manufactured: love, joy, peace, and the rest.
screen: `THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: fruit, not effort. Today, when your one fruit is tested, stay connected instead of straining: one slow breath, then answer. Day one thousand ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some Christians memorize the fruit of the Spirit from Galatians 5:22–23 and use the list to examine their lives.

myth: the verse says "the fruits of the Spirit are"
it says "the fruit of the Spirit is": one fruit, with many flavors.
Paul sets the fruit against "the works of the flesh"
just before the list he names the works of the flesh. works are made; fruit grows.
the fruit, like the gifts, goes to some people and not others
gifts are handed out differently; the fruit is pictured as growing in every life joined to the vine.

fork.setup: you want more patience. by this chapter's picture, what's the way?
options: grit your teeth and force it out.
stay joined to the vine and let it grow.
decide patience just isn't your gift.
fork.reveal: "I am the vine, ye are the branches": in Christian teaching the branch bears fruit by staying joined. the chapter also says "walk in the Spirit": steps, not straining.

original.note: Greek: fruit — singular in Galatians 5:22, "the fruit of the Spirit is."

trapdoor: what you thought: a checklist of nine virtues to work on.
what it means: one fruit with many flavors, grown by the Spirit in a life joined to God, set against the works of the flesh.
what a scholar hears: karpos is singular. the King James words longsuffering, faith, meekness and temperance mean patience, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.

notes: KJV 1769 capitalizes Meekness at the start of verse 23; kept as printed in the quotation.

The KJV order is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance; the index hook and the practice use modern equivalents (patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control). KJV 'gentleness' corresponds to modern 'kindness' and KJV 'meekness' to modern 'gentleness'; the teach glosses meekness as gentleness. Confirm glosses.
'Some readers hear it as one life growing all of these together' is attributed, not stated as the meaning of the singular.
howItsDone mentions Sunday schools using a fruit-tree picture; confirm or cut.
The trapdoor says 'nine virtues' in the 'what you thought' floor only; the KJV list does name nine items.

Editor pass: 'Paul handed out gifts' corrected to 'listed' (the Spirit gives them); the claim that the fruit is for everyone is now attributed to some readers; howItsDone no longer claims Christians 'often' memorize it, and the unsourced Sunday-school detail is cut.
Audit (2026-10-02): hook said Paul writes to 'a different church, in Galatia'; Galatians 1:2 addresses 'the churches of Galatia' (plural). Corrected.
